tools.title: AI Prompts I Keep Coming Back To
tools.summary_raw: Eight simple AI prompt formulas to beat the blank page, plan projects, check facts, copyedit, and critique your work. Perfect for ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.
tools.content_text: Customize these eight prompts rather than building a huge collection When it comes to prompts, you don’t need hundreds. A handful of simple ones can help you clarify thoughts, challenge assumptions, understand complex ideas, and organize plans. The eight flexible prompts below help with a surprising range of these kinds of everyday tasks. Customize the ones most relevant to you. Share How to Make the Most of These Prompts Use them with whatever AI platform you prefer. Try them with free, private AI tools like Duck.ai and Lumo , or top models like ChatGPT , Claude , or Gemini . Tweak the wording . Add constraints and specify your preferred format or style, so it understands what matters to you. The more context and examples you give a model, the better. Exact wording matters less. Copy and customize. I’ve put the full versions in a free prompt library (I made with ChatGPT Sites ). Personalize the prompts and copy them into your preferred AI tool. Subscribe now 1. Interview Me 🎙️ Act as a thorough interviewer. Interview me thoughtfully and creatively about [topic/ project/ idea]. Start by asking me for a quick summary of what I’d like to be interviewed about and why. 1. Ask if there are particular questions I already have in mind. 2. Build a list of questions and check in with me about them. 3. Then ask one question at a time and wait for my response. 4. Ask thoughtful follow-up questions based on what I share. Adapt the questions as you go.… Use this to: Clarify your own jumbled ideas . Having questions to respond to forces you to organize your thoughts. Get past a blank page. Evade writer’s block one reply at a time. Instead of facing a giant topic, you’re just responding to one small query. Ask for: Probing follow-up questions that push you to go deeper or to be more clear, specific, or vivid in your responses. A summary or transcript of your responses at the end of the interview. ChatGPT and Claude give me a document I can review, edit, and print. I use this tactic to: Prepare to teach a new topic . It helps me clarify my own thinking about what learning outcomes are most important or what examples might work well. Get started on a new writing project. It helps me document and organize what’s already on my mind. I often dictate my responses rather than typing to allow my thoughts to flow freely. ( Why I use Voice AI ). 2. Challenge My Thinking 🤔 Help me explore unusual, creative, unconventional approaches to [topic/ challenge/ issue]. First, briefly summarize the conventional wisdom for this topic/situation. Then, provide five surprising, unexpected, or innovative alternatives. For each, explain the underlying rationale and potential benefits. Include perspectives from distinct disciplines or domains that might offer nuanced insights I haven’t considered… Use this to: Catch potential blind spots or holes in your argument Expand your perspective Ask for: An assessment of what a tough editor would say are the weakest parts. market.title: A-lehdet speeds up AI adoption with an in-house short video script creator
market.summary_raw: The Finnish publisher’s custom-built tool streamlines the ideation phase in creating social media videos, helping print and digital journalists turn their articles into engaging short-form content.
market.content_text: About the publisher : A-lehdet is a Finnish publisher best known for its portfolio of magazines that cover current affairs, living, design, health, culture and lifestyle. Beyond print, the group has diversified into digital media, influencer marketing, and e-commerce. Founded in 1933 with the launch of its flagship periodical Apu, the company remains family-owned to this day. Streamlining social video production As news publishers increasingly use social media for video distribution, many newsrooms face new challenges that are upending traditional workflows. From writing to editing, the process of creating video content can add pressure on an already busy newsroom, particularly if the publisher has little background or few resources dedicated to video production. This was the issue that Milla Kukkonen decided to work on during her participation in NextGen AI Leaders , a WAN-IFRA programme in partnership with the Google News Initiative. The programme is designed to help young media leaders reach the next stage in their careers through responsible AI deployment and strategic leadership. In her job as Executive Producer at A-lehdet, Kukkonen has seen how much work transforming an article into a short-form video represents. A particular challenge she had identified was coming up with a strong “hook” that distils the article into an interesting question and captures the viewer’s attention from the start. Using Google AI Studio, she began working on a video scripting assistant, also involving her colleagues in the editorial department for their feedback. A working prototype was already finished before the NextGen AI Leaders programme ended. “It was energising to see how quickly you can create things,” she said. Finding the right opening Kukkonen’s solution allows users to upload their source material (an article or an interview) and generates suggestions on how a video script based on it could be structured, including an attention-grabbing opening. More broadly, mobile video is playing an increasingly important role in A-lehdet’s content strategy, and the new tool supports this by simplifying the process of journalists producing their own videos. The publisher also works with a wide roster of freelancers, and the tool makes it easier to turn externally created articles into videos for social media distribution. “Our aim is to increase mobile video production so that all writers can independently create videos. That’s the need I wanted to address with this tool: to help people script, edit and publish videos on their own,” Kukkonen said. She developed the initial prototype using Google AI Studio, but its features have now been transferred into ChatGPT, bringing them into the AI environment that is used across the company. market.title: Reuters Institute’s Nic Newman on where publishers are seeing growth
market.summary_raw: "Any discussion about monetisation needs to recognise that the way people are accessing news these days is changing. And what people value is also changing," says Nic Newman.
market.content_text: Today, many traditional news publishers are “really rethinking a lot of fundamental things and less about pure reach and more about relationships – about how you build loyalty,” said Newman, Senior Research Associate at Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at Oxford University. News publishers as a whole have seen substantial growth in their subscription businesses during the past decade, and subscription revenue remains a top priority for many. However, “now, we’re in this what you might call a ‘subscription shelf,’ and many publishers are feeling this,” he noted. As a result, today, the focus is increasingly about delivering value, he said, and the questions are along the lines of “how do you build that value in different ways? How do you retain your subscribers by putting more value in? That’s why we’re seeing more bundling, combination of news and lifestyle content being one strategy for that.” Likewise, if publishers are now reaching their likely peak subscriber numbers, then how can they get more out of those subscribers? “One of the things that we see is putting in more premium layers, and trying to increase that average revenue per user (ARPU),” Newman said. WAN-IFRA Members can replay this session and others from Digital Media Europe on our Knowledge Hub. The rise of aggregators and fandom When looking at the overall market of what subscribers are paying for, there are some areas that are clearly increasing, Newman noted. “Firstly the rise of aggregators. And I think that with AI, we will probably see more aggregators as well. Things like Apple News playing an increasingly important role in countries like the UK, Canada, the United States and Germany as well,” he said. A lot of the growth that Reuters Institute is seeing now is around products like video podcasts and newsletters “as businesses in their own right,” such as ones coming from individual Substackers. In addition, “some of the new models are more about fandom. They’re more about shows, putting the talent at the heart and then around that core proposition, you can then build out these different out-puts.” Take Goalhanger for example. “Goalhanger started as a podcast company. It doesn’t call itself a podcast company any more: it does audio, it does video, it does TV. They’re investing in text. They’re investing in newsletters. And then around that, all of these different revenue models: Membership, licensing, brand partnerships. And it’s not an either-or, it’s all of those things together, including ticket sales,” Newman said. In September, Goalhanger organised a large festival at the Southbank Centre in London. Nearly two dozen sessions featured the company’s “hosts coming together and really building those relationships. And making significant amounts of money, too.” Originally a podcast company, Goalhanger has evolved to working in a variety of ways, including events: “They’re really building around that talent and the outputs,” Newman said.
